findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "authentication", "authorization").
findings.evidence: Definition: IAM is the global AWS service that decides who (authentication) can do what on which resource (authorization); principals are users, roles and the root account
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: Access Analyzer and last accessed data are named as the answer to 'what permissions does a role really use' but never explained.
findings.evidence: 'Real permissions used? Access Analyzer, last accessed data'
findings.fix: Add one line saying last accessed data shows which services and actions an identity actually called, and Access Analyzer can generate a least-privilege policy from CloudTrail activity. Use that to trim unused permissions.

findings.summary: One bullet holds two ideas: the Deny conditions and the override rule.
findings.evidence: "Deny on aws:SourceIp or MFA false blocks access even if another policy allows it"
findings.fix: Split it into two bullets: "Deny can use conditions such as aws:SourceIp or MFA false" and "A matching Deny blocks access even if another policy allows it".

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "definition", "security").
findings.evidence: Definition: MFA adds a second factor (virtual TOTP app, FIDO2 security key or hardware token) on top of the password; the root account is the all-powerful email-based identity created with the account
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "automatically", "credentials").
findings.evidence: Comparison: access keys are long-lived (AKIA...) and leak through code and git; role credentials are temporary (ASIA... plus session token) and expire automatically, so prefer roles for EC2, Lambda and CI
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "applications", "credentials").
findings.evidence: Interview Point: Why should the root account have no access keys? When do you still need an access key? How do you enforce MFA with a policy? How do applications on EC2 get credentials without keys?
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: The outline's interview points for this section are missing: why root gets no keys, when an access key is still needed, and how EC2 apps get credentials without keys.
findings.evidence: Page 3 has sections 1-4 plus a 'Keys hygiene' note and no interview block. The only hint is the table row 'Use for | local CLI only'.
findings.fix: Add an 'Interview Point' block. Cover: root keys give full-account power and cannot be scoped; keys are still needed for local CLI or external systems that cannot assume a role; EC2 apps get credentials from an instance profile role via STS.

findings.summary: The key-rotation rule sits under the "Example: Enforce MFA" section after the code, so it is unrelated to that section and easy to miss.
findings.evidence: "4. Example: Enforce MFA ... Keys hygiene Rotate or delete any access key unused for 90 days."
findings.fix: Move the rule into section 3 "Keys vs Roles" or into its own numbered section.

findings.summary: The Root-only bullet packs several separate tasks into one line.
findings.evidence: "Root-only: change root email or password, close account, restore locked-out IAM admin"
findings.fix: Make it a short list with one task per bullet.

findings.summary: The heading "Policy Types" is reused for a different classification than page 2 (managed vs inline instead of identity vs resource-based), which can confuse a learner skimming for the term.
findings.evidence: Page 2: "2. Policy types ... Identity-based | Resource-based | Permission boundary | SCP" vs page 4: "2. Policy Types ... AWS managed | Customer managed | Inline"
findings.fix: Rename page 4's section to "Managed vs Inline Policies" and page 2's to "Policy Types by Scope".

findings.summary: The cheat sheet says everyone else should use roles or IAM Identity Center, but page 3 says daily work uses an IAM user or IAM Identity Center.
findings.evidence: Page 3: "Daily work: IAM user or IAM Identity Center" vs page 5: "Everyone else: roles or IAM Identity Center"
findings.fix: Use the same wording on both pages, for example "Daily work: IAM Identity Center or roles; IAM users only when needed".

findings.summary: The quiz answer depends on the service principal ec2.amazonaws.com, which the chapter never teaches. Trust policy is also used on pages 1 and 4 before it is defined.
findings.evidence: 'The trust policy must name ec2.amazonaws.com as Principal.' Page 1 only says 'Principals named in its trust policy', and page 4 says 'Role needs a trust policy and a permissions policy'.
findings.fix: On page 1 or 4, define a trust policy as the resource-based policy on a role that names who may assume it. Show a short example with Principal {"Service":"ec2.amazonaws.com"} and Action sts:AssumeRole.

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "geographic", "resources").
findings.evidence: A Region is an isolated geographic area with 3+ AZs; an AZ is one or more data centres. Most resources are regional or AZ-scoped, and IAM is global.
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "private", "network").
findings.evidence: A VPC is your private network inside one Region and spans all its AZs. Pick a primary CIDR between /16 and /28, such as 10.0.0.0/16, and keep it clear of other VPCs and on-prem ranges.
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: CIDR is used in the scope map and mistakes before any explanation of what it is or what /16 or /28 means.
findings.evidence: "Primary CIDR between /16 and /28, e.g. 10.0.0.0/16" and "Why CIDR for peering? Overlapping ranges cannot be routed."
findings.fix: Add a short line to the scope map: CIDR is an IP range written as address/prefix length; a smaller number means a bigger range, so /16 is about 65k addresses and /28 is 16.

findings.summary: The CIDR bullets are tacked onto the scope table, and the mistakes are fragments with no stated consequence.
findings.evidence: "Primary CIDR between /16 and /28, e.g. 10.0.0.0/16" after the table; "Default VPC used for production"
findings.fix: Give CIDR its own short heading, and phrase each mistake with its consequence, e.g. 'Default VPC in production: no deliberate CIDR or subnet design'.

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "automatically", "horizontally").
findings.evidence: An IGW is free, horizontally scaled, and lets instances reach the internet only if they also have a public or Elastic IP. A zonal NAT gateway sits in a public subnet with an Elastic IP (a regional NAT gateway needs no public subnet and spans AZs automatically) and gives private subnets outbound-only internet via 0.0.0.0/0 -> nat-id.
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: One bullet packs two unrelated rules, and the public/private definition is split across bullets.
findings.evidence: "One route table per subnet; longest prefix wins"
findings.fix: Split into two bullets: one route table per subnet, and longest prefix wins.

findings.summary: "Ephemeral ports" is used as the reason NACLs need a return-traffic rule, but the chapter never says what they are.
findings.evidence: "Stateless: allow replies, ports 1024-65535" and "A custom NACL without the outbound ephemeral range breaks replies." Page 6 then relies on it: "replies leave on the client's ephemeral port."
findings.fix: On page 3, add one line: the client picks a random high port (1024-65535) as its source port, and the server's reply goes back to that port, so a stateless NACL must allow that range outbound.

findings.summary: Bullets hold more than one idea, and the SG/NACL example diagram has no visible flow or direction.
findings.evidence: "Allow only; default deny in, allow all out"; "Stateless: allow replies, ports 1024-65535"; "Internet / Web SG / DB SG"
findings.fix: Split each into one-idea bullets, and draw the example as Internet -> Web SG (443) -> DB SG (5432 from web-SG) with arrows.

findings.summary: The T-type credit behaviour is stated twice with slightly different instance lists, and a third time in the interview point.
findings.evidence: "T-types burst on CPU credits; standard mode throttles when empty, unlimited (T3/T4g default) bills surplus" / "Unlimited mode (T3/T3a/T4g/T8i) bills surplus" / "Credits out? Standard: throttles to baseline. Unlimited (T3/T3a/T4g default)..."
findings.fix: State it once as a two-row Standard vs Unlimited table with a single instance list, and keep one short interview line.

findings.summary: The page is overloaded and mixes topics. A launch-checklist bullet sits inside the pricing block, and the mistakes are one prose sentence holding three ideas.
findings.evidence: "Launch with SG, key pair, subnet, IAM instance profile, not keys" under Pricing; "Stopped instances still pay for EBS; unattached Elastic IPs bill; Spot is wrong for stateful databases."
findings.fix: Move the launch bullet under AMIs or a short Launch heading, and split the mistakes into three one-line bullets.

findings.summary: The troubleshooting chain is written as one dense line where a layered diagram or list would be easier to scan.
findings.evidence: "Internet to private DB: IGW (not attached), route table (no route), NACL (deny, no ephemeral ports), SG (no allow rule), instance (not listening)."
findings.fix: Show it as an ordered list or a flow: IGW -> route table -> NACL -> SG -> instance, with the failure cause on each line.

findings.summary: The explanation of why the outbound-443-only NACL breaks replies is worded backwards: replies leave from port 443 and are addressed to the client's ephemeral port.
findings.evidence: NACLs are stateless: replies leave on the client's ephemeral port.
findings.fix: Reword to: "NACLs are stateless: replies go from port 443 to the client's ephemeral port, so the outbound rule must allow destination ports 1024-65535."

findings.summary: The Everyday Commands section shows four commands with no line first saying what they do.
findings.evidence:
3. Everyday Commands
bash
aws s3 cp file s3://bucket/key
aws s3 ls s3://bucket/prefix/

findings.fix: Say "Glacier Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive objects need a restore before GET; Glacier Instant Retrieval is read directly in milliseconds." Make the same change on pages 1 and 6.

findings.summary: The Deep Archive retrieval times '~12h / ~48h' are never labeled as Standard and Bulk, so a learner cannot tell which tier each number belongs to.
findings.evidence: Deep Archive | archive | 180d | ~12h / ~48h
findings.fix: Write 'Standard ~12h / Bulk ~48h' in the Get column, and give the Flexible tiers rough times (Expedited minutes, Standard hours, Bulk longer) so the Expedited/Standard/Bulk list has meaning.

findings.summary: NoncurrentVersionExpiration and 'old versions' are used before versioning, current versus noncurrent, and delete markers are introduced on page 4.
findings.evidence: Also set AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload, NoncurrentVersionExpiration ... Old versions? Expire noncurrent versions

findings.summary: The Get column and the retrieval tiers are shown without saying what they mean, so the '~12h / ~48h' values can't be read.

findings.fix: Rename the column to 'Retrieval time'. Label the Deep Archive values (Standard ~12h, Bulk ~48h). Give a speed for each Flexible tier or drop the tier list.

lists versions and delete markers

findings.summary: The Block Public Access bullet packs four separate switches into one line, and the ARN failure bullet is cryptic.

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "throughput", "workloads").

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "configurable", "transaction").

d111abcdef8.cloudfront.net
inherits target's TTL
Zone recreated?
Update the registrar NS to the new hosted zone's NS. Stale NS means DNS resolves nowhere"
findings.fix: Show the example as a small table (Name | Type | Target | TTL) and put the mistake in a labelled callout: 'Zone recreated -> new NS set -> update registrar NS'.

findings.summary: The alias targets are split across three bullets, and one of them holds two ideas.
findings.evidence: "Targets: CloudFront, ALB/NLB, API Gateway, S3 website endpoint\nAlso Elastic Beanstalk, or another record in the same zone\nAn alias cannot point to an EC2 DNS name"
findings.fix: Merge the targets into one list and make the EC2 limitation a separate 'Not allowed' line.

findings.summary: Geoproximity routing is described as requiring Traffic Flow, which is outdated.
findings.evidence: Geoproximity: needs Traffic Flow, shifted with bias
findings.fix: Say geoproximity records (with a bias) can be created directly as a routing policy on a record, as well as in Traffic Flow, and keep the bias explanation.

findings.summary: The failover flow is written as two separate arrow lines instead of a single branching diagram.
findings.evidence: "Primary healthy? --yes--> Serve primary\nPrimary healthy? --no--> Serve secondary"
findings.fix: Draw it as one decision node with yes and no branches.

findings.summary: The Simple row says 'no health checks on it', which is ambiguous. The routing-policy table also omits Failover, Geolocation and Geoproximity, so the page's policies are split between a table and bullets.
findings.evidence: "Simple | one or more values, random order | no health checks on it"; Geoproximity: "needs Traffic Flow, shifted with bias"
findings.fix: Rephrase to 'no health checks per value' and extend the table to cover Failover, Geolocation and Geoproximity with their key fact.

findings.summary: Code appears before the idea that explains it, and two commands share one idea line.
findings.evidence: "Create or update a record: UPSERT inside change.json" followed directly by the bash block; "Check an answer with dig, or ask Route 53 itself"
findings.fix: State one-line intent for each command. Split the check line into 'dig: what a resolver returns' and 'test-dns-answer: what Route 53 would answer'.

findings.summary: The 'Common mistakes' block holds two ideas in one line, and the health-check fixes are scattered across the page.
findings.evidence: "A failover or weighted record with no health check keeps sending traffic to a dead endpoint. An alias record can use Evaluate Target Health instead of a separate check."
findings.fix: Split into two bullets: the mistake (no health check attached) and the alternative (alias + Evaluate Target Health).

findings.summary: The origin flow is a linear list with ambiguous labels, so the cache layers are hard to follow. The 'Origin group' bullet is unclear about what triggers failover.
findings.evidence:
"Viewer
request
Edge location
hit: serve
Regional edge cache
edge miss
Origin
cache miss"; "Origin group = failover to a secondary origin on 5xx or 4xx"
findings.fix: Draw a clear left-to-right flow: Viewer -> Edge (hit: serve) -> Regional edge cache (hit: serve) -> Origin, with miss labels on each arrow. Say which status codes trigger origin group failover.

findings.summary: The 'Behaviours' bullet crams four settings into one line, and the cache policy vs origin request policy table is given without the idea stated first.
findings.evidence: "Picks origin, allowed methods, cache policy, viewer protocol policy (redirect HTTP to HTTPS)"; "Policy | Forwarded to origin | In cache key"
findings.fix: List the settings a behaviour picks as separate short bullets and add a one-line lead-in: 'Origin request policy forwards without changing the cache key'.

findings.summary: The TTL bullet holds several rules at once, and the 'First 1,000 paths/month free' fact sits in the invalidation block as an unattached line.
findings.evidence: "Origin max-age or s-maxage is honoured, clamped to policy Minimum TTL and Maximum TTL"; "First 1,000 paths/month free"
findings.fix: Present TTL resolution as a short ordered list or table (origin header -> clamp to Min/Max; no header -> Default TTL 86400s). Move the free-path allowance into its own cost note.

findings.summary: The cheat sheet repeats the invalidation code block, and the Route 53 record and policy tables drop facts that the chapter treated as important.
findings.evidence: "aws cloudfront create-invalidation \\\n  --distribution-id E123 \\\n  --paths \"/index.html\" \"/img/*\""; "Policy | Key fact" omits Geoproximity
findings.fix: Drop the repeated command and keep the one-line rule 'invalidate only when the URL cannot change'. Add Geoproximity (Traffic Flow, bias) to the policy table.

findings.summary: The container-sharing guidance is split into bullets plus a table, and the key rule is mixed into one bullet.
findings.evidence: Containers in a task share one network namespace and lifecycle
findings.fix: Split into two bullets: 'share one network namespace' and 'share one lifecycle (start and stop together)'.

findings.summary: The ':latest' mistake is told as a chain of text lines instead of a small flow, and one bullet holds several ideas.
findings.evidence: Old revision pulls the new broken image: no rollback
findings.fix: Show the chain as a short diagram (revision 6 and revision 7 both point to :latest, which now points to the broken image) and split the consequence from the 'no rollback' conclusion.

findings.summary: The ECS hierarchy is stated as a list of boxes without showing the nesting or the relationship direction.
findings.evidence: Cluster holds services / Service keeps N tasks / Task running instance / Task definition the blueprint
findings.fix: Draw it as a nested or arrow diagram: Cluster > Service > Task, with Task definition feeding Task.

findings.summary: The 'Mistake' section is a single dense sentence holding two causes and two symptoms.
findings.evidence: Task stuck in PROVISIONING or STOPPED: no route to ECR (private subnet without NAT or VPC endpoints) or the execution role lacks permission.
findings.fix: Use a two-row cause/fix table or two bullets: 'No route to ECR: add NAT or VPC endpoints' and 'Execution role lacks pull permission: grant it'.

findings.summary: Bullets hold more than one idea, and the rollout/rollback settings are not explained.
findings.evidence: Rolling update: minimumHealthyPercent and maxPercent
findings.fix: Give each setting its own bullet with its meaning (floor of healthy tasks, ceiling of total tasks during a deploy).

findings.summary: The comparison table says Fargate scales to "Any size", which is false and teaches the wrong limit.
findings.evidence: Scale | Any size, no hosts | Very large steady workloads
findings.fix: Change the Fargate cell to "No hosts to scale, but task size is capped (16 vCPU)". Keep EC2 as the pick for very large steady workloads.

findings.summary: The Fargate vs EC2 table cells are mixed: the 'Cost' and 'Scale' rows do not compare like with like, and the Fargate/EC2 explanation is split between bullets and the table.
findings.evidence: Scale | Any size, no hosts | Very large steady workloads
findings.fix: Make the rows parallel (e.g. Scale: 'No hosts to size' vs 'You size and manage the fleet') and move the bullets about patching and capacity providers into table rows.

findings.summary: A bullet holds multiple ideas and the key comparison fact is buried in a prose sentence.
findings.evidence: You pay later in upgrade work (a Kubernetes version gets ~14 months of support), add-ons and networking complexity.
findings.fix: Split into bullets: upgrade work (~14 months support per version), add-on management, networking complexity.

findings.summary: The docker login command is incomplete: it omits the username and `--password-stdin`, so it would not authenticate.
findings.evidence: aws ecr get-login-password | docker login $ECR
findings.fix: Use: aws ecr get-login-password --region $REGION | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin $ECR

findings.summary: The ECR login command is incomplete and would fail as written.
findings.evidence: aws ecr get-login-password | docker login $ECR
findings.fix: Use `aws ecr get-login-password --region $REGION | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin $ECR`.

findings.summary: Commands are shown as a block with several update-service forms and the idea behind them comes after the code.
findings.evidence:
aws ecs update-service --task-definition fam:rev --force-new-deployment
...
update-service points the service at a revision
Redeploy is not rollout
findings.fix: State the one-line idea before the code block, and show register then update-service as separate commands with --force-new-deployment explained in a separate line.

findings.summary: The ALB and security group relationship is a list of labels rather than a followable diagram.
findings.evidence: Internet 80 / 443 ALB group open to internet Task group container port, source = ALB group
findings.fix: Draw arrows: Internet -> (80/443) ALB SG -> (container port) Task SG, labelling the task SG source as the ALB SG.

findings.summary: The cheat sheet shows code before the idea behind it, and repeats the --force-new-deployment mistake text from pages 2 and 5.
findings.evidence:
bash
docker push $ACCT.dkr.ecr.$REGION.amazonaws.com/app:$SHA
...
update-service points the service at the revision
findings.fix: Put the one-line idea ('Push, register, then point the service at the new revision') above the code block.

findings.summary: The debug checklist's 'Check' cells pack several checks into single cells.
findings.evidence: CannotPullContainerError (NAT or endpoints); execution role; missing log group
findings.fix: Split into one row per check, each with its symptom and fix.

findings.summary: Code block appears after the declarative-ordering bullets but is not introduced by a one-line idea, and the minimal template does not show Ref/GetAtt ordering it sits under.
findings.evidence: 3. Declarative Ordering ... yaml Resources: Bucket: Type: AWS::S3::Bucket Outputs: BucketArn: Value: !GetAtt Bucket.Arn
findings.fix: Put the code under its own caption, such as 'Minimal template', placed after a one-line statement that Outputs reads a resource attribute via !GetAtt, or move it to the Template vs Stack section.

findings.summary: The 'Drift and Rollback' section mixes two ideas and the rollback rules are written as text where a small state table would be clearer.
findings.evidence: Drift detection compares live resources with the template: IN_SYNC or DRIFTED / It only detects, it never fixes / Failed create → ROLLBACK_COMPLETE: delete only, no update / Failed update → rolls back to the last good state
findings.fix: Split into 'Drift' and 'Rollback' sections, and show rollback as a table of failed create vs failed update with the resulting state and the allowed action.

findings.summary: The 'Protect Data' section holds unrelated ideas in one flat list, and the grouping label 'Data guards' covers only the first bullets.
findings.evidence: Data guards ... Stack termination protection blocks delete / Nested stacks and exports split large stacks / An export in use cannot be changed or deleted
findings.fix: Put the policies and protections in a table (Control | Protects against), and move nested stacks and exports to their own short section.

findings.summary: The 'Commands and Bootstrap' section has a bullet that joins two ideas, and 'Missing bootstrap' is stated without the error a learner would see.
findings.evidence: cdk bootstrap: once per account/region, creates the CDKToolkit stack
findings.fix: Split into 'Run once per account/region' and 'Creates the CDKToolkit stack', and name the symptom, for example a missing-bootstrap error, on the failure bullet.

findings.summary: The Reserved Instances row is vague and the Savings Plans commitment bullets sit apart from the table they describe.
findings.evidence: Reserved Instances | A specific instance configuration | Commitment discount
findings.fix: Give a real discount figure or range for Reserved Instances, and move the Compute and EC2 Instance Savings Plans lines into the table as sub-rows.

findings.summary: A bullet holds two ideas, and the Cost Explorer section mixes a tool description with an unrelated Budgets capability.
findings.evidence: Budgets | your threshold: cost, usage or Savings Plans coverage; actual or forecasted % | email or SNS
findings.fix: Split the Budgets row into what it measures and when it fires. Move 'Budget actions can apply IAM or SCP restrictions' out of the Cost Explorer list into the Budgets row.

findings.summary: The cheat sheet's CDK flow lists steps as loose lines without showing the order or the command descriptions, and the 'Cost Checklist' last bullet lists five unrelated items.
findings.evidence: Delete idle NAT Gateways, load balancers, EBS volumes, snapshots
findings.fix: Number the CDK steps in one flow line, and split the last checklist item into separate bullets, or group them as 'Delete idle: NAT, load balancers, EBS, snapshots'.

findings.summary: The CDK rename quiz answer relies on removal policy, RETAIN and DESTROY, which the chapter never teaches, and it differs from page 3's 'old resource is replaced'.
findings.evidence: "The old bucket is deleted only if its removal policy is DESTROY. The L2 default is RETAIN, so it stays behind as an orphan." versus page 3: "Changing a construct ID changes the logical ID: the old resource is replaced."
findings.fix: Add a line on page 3 or page 2 explaining that CDK's removal policy maps to DeletionPolicy and that the L2 Bucket default is RETAIN. Reword page 3 to say that a new resource is created and the old one is deleted only if its removal policy allows it. Otherwise drop the removal-policy sentences from the quiz answer.
